items.title: Two different questions: may this role act, and on whose data
items.body:
Access control in this app answers two separate questions, and mixing them up is the classic mistake.

- **Permission**: may this role do the action at all? For example, may a Teacher grade?
- **Scope**: on *which* records? A Teacher may grade, but only students in sections they teach.

The scope module says this in its own header comment. Read the `switch` in `buildStudentScope` role by role: each `case` is one rule in plain data. Note what it returns, every branch included, and ask why it returns that kind of value rather than filtering students after they are fetched.

Also note where each check lives: in the page, or inside the Server Action that does the work. Keep both questions in mind when you read the "still stands" table in 04.

excerpts.quote: * This is a different question from canPerformAction, and conflating the two is * the most common authorization mistake there is. Permissions answer "may this * role grade?"; scoping answers "whose work?". A Teacher may grade, but not * every student's; a Parent may view a profile, but only their own child's.

items.title: Leaving DeadLettered needs an explicit requeue
items.body:
`JOB_TRANSITIONS` lists where each job state may go next. `DeadLettered` may go only to `Queued`, marked "requeue only". `requeueJob` refuses any job whose state cannot move to Queued, and when it succeeds it sets `status: 'Queued'` and `attempts: 0`, giving the job a fresh attempt budget.

- "Never": DeadLettered does have one outgoing edge, to Queued.
- "Automatically when attempts < maxAttempts": a worker may only pick up `RUNNABLE_STATUSES` (Queued, Failed, Retrying); DeadLettered is not in that list.
- "Retry Now runs it at once, as before Story 3": running it directly was the old bug (B6). Now the page and worker share `canRunJob`, which rejects DeadLettered.

items.title: A dropped row still blocks re-enrolment
items.body:
Three facts combine. The schema puts `@@unique([studentId, classSectionId])` on Enrollment, so one student can only ever have one row per section. Dropping a student updates that row to `status: 'Dropped'`; it does not delete it. Then the enrol action looks the row up with `findUnique` (any status) and passes `hasExistingEnrollment: !!existing`, and the rule rejects with "already enrolled or waitlisted". 04 adds that Story 12's waitlist promotion now relies on there being only one row.

- "A second Enrolled row is created": the unique constraint makes a second row impossible.
- "Dropping deleted the row": the drop action sets the status to Dropped.
- "Waitlisted automatically": the rule returns `canWaitlist: false` for this case.

items.title: The claim lives in the write's WHERE
items.body:
If a worker reads a row, sees Queued, and then updates it, two workers can both read Queued before either writes, and both run the job. `claimJob` avoids this by putting the status check **inside** the write: `updateMany` only changes the row if its id matches **and** its status is still runnable. The first write flips it to Running, so the second write no longer matches and returns count 0. `claimJob` returns `result.count === 1`, so exactly one worker wins.

- "updateMany is faster, so the race is too small": the comment says the guard must live in the WHERE so the database decides; speed is not the fix.
- "updateMany locks the table until the job finishes": the write finishes immediately; nothing is held while the job runs.
- "update cannot increment": `attempts: { increment: 1 }` is ordinary Prisma; the real problem is that `update` matches on id alone.

excerpts.quote: * This is the whole reason a queue is not just "SELECT then UPDATE". Two * workers reading the same Queued row would both see it as runnable and both * execute it. The guard has to live in the WHERE clause of the write, so the * database decides the winner:
where: { id: jobId, status: { in: RUNNABLE_STATUSES } },

* else sees 0 because the row no longer matches the status filter. `update` * could not express this — it matches on the id alone and would happily * overwrite a row another worker had already claimed.

items.title: An unknown role sees no students
items.body:
`buildStudentScope` is a `switch` over `session.role`. Admin, SchoolManager and Viewer get `{}` (everyone); Teacher, Advisor, Student and Parent each get a narrower `where`. Any other string falls to the `default` branch, which returns `{ id: '__no_access__' }`. No real student has that id, so the query matches nothing. The comment calls this failing closed: the role column is a plain string, so an unexpected value is possible, and the safe answer is "see nothing".

- "The request throws": there *is* a `default` branch, and it returns a value instead of throwing.
- "All students, like Admin": only the three unscoped roles return the empty object; unknown roles do not reach that case.
- "Only their own sections, like a Teacher": that is the Teacher case, which needs the role to be exactly 'Teacher'.

excerpts.quote: default: // Unknown role: see nothing. Failing closed is the only safe default for // a switch over a plain string column. return { id: '__no_access__' };

items.title: Start here: read the gotchas, then what changed
items.body:
This pack is about EduOps, a school back-office app built with Next.js, Prisma and SQLite. The quizzes ask how the code behaves **today**, after a 19-story build, so the order you read in matters.

1. `fabledocs/README.md` - one table that says which file to read when.
2. `fabledocs/01-how-this-app-works.md` - what the product is and how a request flows. Read it end to end.
3. `fabledocs/02-codebase-gotchas.md` - a list of traps found in the code **as it was first imported**. It is kept unedited on purpose, so some items are now history.
4. `fabledocs/04-what-changed.md` - the reconciliation: one table of gotchas that are fixed, one of gotchas that still stand. Read it right after 02, and when the two disagree, 04 wins.
5. `docs/architectural-cartographer/02-mid-level-engineer.md` - architecture, the support-notes filter and the "no client state" idea.

When a guide quotes a line number, open the file in `src/` and read the real code: several quizzes hinge on one line.

excerpts.quote: > **This document describes the codebase as originally imported** (commit > `chore: import EduOps application baseline`). Many of these findings have since been > fixed by the 19-story build — see [`04-what-changed.md`](04-what-changed.md) for what is > still true. It is kept unedited on purpose: the *reasoning* about why each one mattered > is the teaching material, and rewriting history would destroy it.

**Read `02-codebase-gotchas.md` alongside this file.** That document describes the codebase *as imported*, and it is still the right starting point for understanding why things are the way they are — but the table below says which of its findings are now history.

items.title: No graded work means a 100% 'Excellent'
items.body:
When the loop finishes with `totalPointsPossible <= 0` (no graded or missing work), `calculateSectionGrade` returns early with `percentage: 100` and `classification: 'Excellent'`. Gotcha B1 calls it a real product choice, "innocent until proven guilty", with a real cost: a new student shows Low risk everywhere and is invisible to the risk system. 04 says it is deliberate and pinned by a characterisation test.

- "0% Failing": the code returns 100, not 0.
- "null, badge hidden": the function always returns an object with a number.
- "NaN": the early return happens **before** the division on line 75, so zero is never divided by zero.

items.title: The cast exposes an unreachable branch
items.body:
Read the filter top to bottom. The second line returns `true` for Admin **and** SchoolManager. After that line TypeScript narrows `activeUser.role` so it can no longer be 'Admin', and comparing it to 'Admin' would be a type error. The cast to `string` silences that error, but the narrowing was telling the truth: the AdminOnly branch can never return true. Gotcha C5 names the result: AdminOnly notes are already visible to SchoolManager through the early return, and the AdminOnly line itself is dead.

- "Widens the check to Advisors": the line still compares against 'Admin' only.
- "Admin stored in lowercase": the earlier line compares 'Admin' with no cast and works.
- "role is typed any": if it were `any`, TypeScript would not narrow it and no cast would be needed.

excerpts.quote: if (activeUser.role === 'Admin' || activeUser.role === 'SchoolManager') return true; if (note.visibility === 'TeacherOnly' && activeUser.role === 'Teacher') return true; if (note.visibility === 'AdvisorOnly' && activeUser.role === 'Advisor') return true; if (note.visibility === 'AdminOnly' && (activeUser.role as string) === 'Admin') return true;

items.title: Why scoping is a WHERE fragment, not a JS filter
items.body:
The header comment of `scope.ts` explains the choice. If you fetch every student and then filter in JavaScript, the code looks fine until somebody adds a `take`, a `count` or an aggregate. Those run in the database, before your filter, so the numbers include rows the viewer was never allowed to see, and the leak is a quietly wrong total. Putting the rule into the query itself means no later code can forget it. 04 points to PR #15 for the same reasoning.

- "JS filters run on the client and can't read the cookie": these are server components; the guide's reason is about counts and limits, not where code runs.
- "Prisma crashes without loaded relations": nothing in the guide says so.
- "Next.js caches WHERE fragments": the comment is about correctness, not speed or caching.

excerpts.quote: * The output is a Prisma WHERE fragment, not a filter function, and that is * deliberate. Fetching everything and then filtering in JavaScript "works" * until someone adds a `take`, a `count`, or an aggregate — at which point the * numbers are computed over rows the user was never allowed to see, and the * leak is a total that is silently too high. Push the constraint into the query * and it cannot be forgotten downstream.

items.title: A mid-loop failure leaves a half-recorded register
items.body:
`recordAttendanceAction` walks the records with a plain `for` loop. For each student it runs a `findUnique`, an `upsert` and an audit write, each as its own database statement. Nothing wraps the loop, so when student 17 fails, the 16 earlier rows are already committed and stay; students 17-30 are never written. Gotcha B12 describes exactly this, and 04 confirms there is still no `$transaction` anywhere.

- "All 30 rows, upsert retries": `upsert` does not retry; an error simply stops the loop.
- "Only the audit rows": the audit write comes **after** each upsert, not before.
- "Nothing, it runs in db.$transaction": there is no transaction in this code base.

excerpts.quote: `recordAttendanceAction` (`actions.ts:228-270`) loops over students doing an `upsert` plus an audit write per student. A failure halfway through leaves a half-recorded register. There is no `db.$transaction` anywhere in the codebase.

items.title: The database is the state: server pages, actions and revalidation
items.body:
If you come from React single-page apps you will look for `useState` or Redux. You will not find it for domain data. In this app a page is a server component: it reads exactly what it needs from SQLite through Prisma, renders HTML and sends it.

When something changes, a **Server Action** in `src/app/actions.ts` runs the business rule, writes the database, records an audit event or job, and calls `revalidatePath()` so Next.js re-runs the page with fresh data.

The only global state is the user session, held in a cookie and resolved on every request. That is why you should trace a feature as page -> action -> domain rule -> Prisma, and why the business rules in `src/packages/domain/rules/` are plain, testable functions.

excerpts.quote: **There is no client-side state management for domain data.** In traditional SPAs, you fetch data from an API and store it in Redux. Here, the "State" is simply the SQLite database. Next.js fetches the exact data required for the page directly from the DB on the server, renders the HTML, and sends it to the client. If data changes via an Action, `revalidatePath()` tells Next.js to re-run the server component and push fresh HTML. The only "global state" is the user session, which is stored in a cookie and resolved on every server request via `getActiveUser()`.

items.title: A bare date and a timestamp are two keys
items.body:
The unique key includes `date`, a full DateTime. The action does `new Date(date)`. `'2026-05-22'` becomes midnight UTC; `'2026-05-22T09:00:00Z'` becomes 09:00 the same day. Those are different DateTime values, so the upsert finds no match for the second one and creates a new row. Gotcha B11: idempotency holds only while every writer sends a bare `YYYY-MM-DD`.

- "Prisma compares by calendar day": the key is an exact DateTime; nothing rounds it to a day.
- "zod rejects the timestamp": the schema only checks that `new Date(v)` parses, and an ISO timestamp parses fine.
- "The schema strips the time": the refine checks the value, it does not change it.

excerpts.quote: const dateFromInput = z .string() .min(1, 'A date is required.') .refine((v) => !Number.isNaN(new Date(v).getTime()), 'Not a valid date.');

`DateTime`. `recordAttendanceAction` does `new Date("2026-05-22")` → midnight UTC, so the upsert is idempotent **as long as every writer uses a bare `YYYY-MM-DD` string**. Pass a date with a time component and you'll create a duplicate row for the same day.
